name: Red Wine
lede: Red wine is a deep crimson-maroon named for the drink, and, as Pastoureau notes, even the drink is not really red but dark.

sections.title: A name that means dark
sections.body: The historian Pastoureau points out that "red wine" and "white wine" classify more than they describe: white wine is never white but yellow, golden or greenish, and red wine is not red but dark [1]. In the Middle Ages red was the archetypal color of wine, although white wine was drunk more often, and Communion wine was mixed with water and looked lighter than its symbol [2]. Paterson's dictionary lists wine-colour as the color of red wine, and wine-dark as Homer's phrase for the sea [3].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
Our library files Red Wine from the xkcd color survey, with [[burgundy]] as its nearest everyday name, 5.9 units away, and [[claret]] as a close neighbor [4]. Related words include [[maroon]] and [[oxblood]], though these run browner or darker [4].

Paterson also notes that tasters given a white wine stained red described its flavor as that of a red wine, so the color changed the taste they reported [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Red Wine is nearly absent from painting: only 2 of 23,781 archive works carry it, among them a 1510 *Head of a Woman* [5]. The phrase in print has risen since 1980 and peaks in the 2010s, in step with wine writing rather than art [6]. As ever, the data are photographs of aged, varnished paintings [5].

questions.q: What does Pastoureau say "red" in red wine really means?

openers: Red wine is not red but dark, and white wine is never white.

issues: Lede softened from 'rarely the color of its name' to the source's 'not red but dark'
